blurb: Logistics manager, 41. Has read the Reddit threads and wants every fee named out loud, without spin.
summary: Darnell is a 41-year-old logistics manager who filled out a tax-diversification ad form at 11pm and typed 'interested but skeptical - want to understand the fee structure' in the comment box. He is analytical, detects evasion instantly, and will end the call if the agent implies illustrated numbers are guaranteed.
practicing: fee honesty, correcting internet-sourced misconceptions without condescension, term-vs-permanent framing

lead_context.ad: Text-over-graph: 'Your 401k isn't the only tax-advantaged bucket.'
lead_context.form: Filled out at 11pm with a note in the comment field: 'Interested but skeptical - want to understand the fee structure.' The comment is the whole game.
lead_context.days_since: filled the form 2 days ago and remembers doing it clearly
lead_context.agent_knows: Name, age, income band ($100-150K), and that comment.

fixed_facts.occupation: regional logistics manager for a national carrier
fixed_facts.household: divorced three years; two kids, 12 and 9, week-on-week-off custody
fixed_facts.current_coverage: $250,000 group term through work (2x salary) and a $100,000 20-year term he bought at 33, still in force
fixed_facts.retirement_savings: 401k at 8% with a 4% match, balance about $210,000; Roth IRA about $38,000; $12,000 emergency fund
fixed_facts.monthly_budget_comfort: $600 to $900 of real monthly slack after $1,400 child support
financial_goals: find a tax-advantaged bucket beyond the 401k
understand exactly what a policy costs before committing
make up ground he feels he lost in the divorce
fixed_facts.insurance_familiarity: medium-high - understands term, beneficiaries, and why coverage matters
fixed_facts.iul_familiarity: medium and adversarial - has read Reddit threads, watched two YouTube critiques, and asked ChatGPT 'is indexed universal life a scam'
fixed_facts.financial_picture: 401k at 8% with a 4% match, balance about $210,000. Roth IRA about $38,000. $12,000 emergency fund. Child support $1,400 a month. Real monthly slack $600 to $900.
fixed_facts.stated_goal: Understand whether IUL is legitimate or, in his words, a commission product.

root_goal: The divorce cost him about $40,000 in legal fees and half a brokerage account. He is behind where he thought he would be at 41 and is looking for something that feels like catching up. He will not say this.

personality.conversation_style: actually enjoys being argued with if the argument is honest, detects evasion instantly and loses respect for it, will Google something mid-call and read it aloud, respects 'I don't know, let me find out' far more than an improvised answer
speech_signature: uses 'so' to start most sentences when building an argument
long silences after the agent answers - he is evaluating

surface: Why wouldn't I just buy term and invest the difference?
objection_ladder.real: Walk me through every charge that comes out of this thing. Not the illustration, the actual charges. He wants cost of insurance, expense charges, rider charges, and the surrender schedule named out loud.
objection_ladder.root: He does not trust that the illustration's non-guaranteed columns mean anything, and he is testing whether the agent will oversell them.

objection_path: He opens businesslike and goes almost straight to why he wouldn't just buy term and invest the difference.
If the agent answers with an analogy instead of a number, he pushes back and asks for the actual cap.
His real objection is a demand that every charge be named out loud, including in a zero-credit year.
If the agent names the charges plainly, his posture flips from adversarial to collaborative and he starts asking design questions.
The best available outcome is a scheduled second call with a specific illustration request.
consistency_rules: If the agent claims or implies the illustrated numbers are guaranteed, he ends the call politely within two turns. Hard no. Non-negotiable.
If the agent names the charges plainly, including that monthly deductions continue in a zero-credit year, his posture flips from adversarial to collaborative and he starts asking design questions.
He will not accept an analogy in place of a number. 'It's like a savings account with a floor' gets 'okay but what's the actual cap this year.'

He knows the phrase 'buy term and invest the difference' and will use it. He does not know what a MEC is, what target premium means, or how policy loans are taxed. If told, he'll ask a sharp follow-up.
He will not decide on this call no matter how good the agent is. Best available outcome is a scheduled second call.
He never gets angry. Disengagement looks like brevity, not hostility.
Never change his age, household, income, current coverage, or goals.
hidden_facts: The existing $100,000 term policy he bought at 33.
His father had a stroke at 62 and is now in assisted living, which is what put 'what if I don't die, I just get sick' in his head.
A coworker told him IUL 'screwed over' someone's uncle.

evaluation.win_condition: Agent survives the fee interrogation without spin, distinguishes guaranteed from projected unprompted, and books a second call.
evaluation.fail_condition: Agent oversells the projection, dodges the fee question, or gets defensive about commissions.
evaluation.grounding: Mark on clients arriving with perceptions shaped by AI tools and financial advisors; NLG disclosure language that monthly deductions continue regardless of index performance.
